story: Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations while serving in the trenches of the First World War, and posted the result to Einstein from the front. He died of illness months later, before anyone understood he had described a black hole.

Roy Kerr found the equations for a spinning black hole in 1963, twelve years after Schwarzschild's still one had been solved. Real black holes all spin, so Kerr's is the one the universe actually uses.

Hawking showed black holes are not entirely black — they leak, very slowly, and eventually evaporate. He set out to disprove the idea and ended up proving it, which he described as the most surprising result of his life.

Roger Penrose worked out that you could throw an object at a spinning black hole, split it in two, and have one half come back with more energy than you sent in. The black hole pays, by spinning slightly slower.

A triangle that looks perfectly solid and cannot exist. Penrose called it impossibility in its purest form and showed it to the artist Escher, who built entire staircases and waterfalls out of the same trick.

Lorentz wrote down the equations before Einstein did, but treated them as a mathematical fix. Einstein took the same equations and said they meant time and space themselves change with speed — which is why relativity is his.

A charged particle moving through a magnetic field gets pushed sideways, at right angles to both its motion and the field. It is the reason electric motors turn and the reason the aurora glows near the poles.

Four equations that between them describe every electric motor, radio wave and beam of light in existence. Feynman said that from a long enough view of history, the nineteenth century would be remembered for these.

A metal shell keeps electric fields out, which is why you are safe inside a car in a lightning storm — the charge runs around the bodywork, not through you. Faraday tested it by sitting in a foil-lined room while assistants zapped it.

Faraday showed that a magnetic field can twist a beam of polarised light. It was the first hard evidence that light and magnetism were connected at all, and it pointed straight at Maxwell's equations twenty years later.

Over lunch at Los Alamos in 1950, Enrico Fermi interrupted a conversation about aliens with one question: where is everybody? The galaxy is old and vast and should be crowded. It looks empty. Nobody has answered him yet.
Even at absolute zero, electrons in a metal are not still — the rules of quantum mechanics forbid them all sitting in the lowest state. The Fermi energy is the level the topmost ones are stuck at.
Fermi called it golden rule number two in his lectures, and the name stuck. He did not discover it — Dirac did — which makes it one of physics' more cheerfully misattributed results.

Feynman replaced pages of algebra with little pictures of particles meeting, scattering and moving on. Older physicists were suspicious of anything so easy to draw. Within a decade nobody could work without them.
Explain the thing to a child. Wherever you stumble is exactly where you do not understand it. Feynman used this on himself constantly, and it remains the cheapest study method ever devised.

Dirac's equation had two solutions, and one of them described a particle with negative energy. Rather than discard it he suggested it was a real particle nobody had found yet. Four years later someone found the positron.

Bose's paper was rejected by a journal. He posted it to Einstein, who translated it into German himself, added his own extension, and got it published. Seventy years later the state of matter they predicted was finally made in a lab.

Satyendra Nath Bose worked out a new way of counting identical particles that behaves nothing like counting ordinary objects. Swap two of them and nothing changes at all — because there is no way even in principle to tell which is which.

Every particle in the universe is either a boson or a fermion, and the bosons are named after Bose. Dirac chose the name. Bose himself never received a Nobel Prize, though at least ten have been awarded for work built on his.

Peter Higgs's paper was rejected in 1964 as being of no obvious relevance to physics. The particle it predicted was found in 2012, and he got the Nobel the following year — forty-eight years after the rejection.

An invisible field filling all of space, which particles drag through like walking in water. The dragging is what we call mass. A writer nicknamed it the God particle; Higgs, an atheist, disliked the name intensely.

C. V. Raman started wondering why the sea is blue on a voyage home from England, and ended up discovering that molecules shift the colour of light that bounces off them. It won him the Nobel Prize in 1930.

Shine a laser at a substance and the light that scatters back carries a fingerprint of exactly which molecules are present. It identifies paint on a masterpiece or a pill in a packet without touching either.

Rudolf Mossbauer found that atoms locked in a crystal can emit gamma rays without recoiling, giving a beam of extraordinary precision. He was a doctoral student, and had a Nobel Prize by the age of thirty-two.
Put an atom in a magnetic field and its spectral lines split apart. Zeeman was reprimanded for wasting laboratory time on the experiment. He won a Nobel Prize for it six years later.

The electric-field twin of the Zeeman effect — spectral lines splitting under voltage rather than magnetism. Johannes Stark won a Nobel for it, then spent his later career attacking the physics of Einstein on political grounds.

Compton bounced X-rays off electrons and found the light lost energy, exactly as if it were made of particles colliding. It was the experiment that made physicists accept the photon as real rather than a bookkeeping trick.

Metals are made of tiny crystal grains, and cracks travel easily inside a grain but struggle to cross a boundary. Make the grains smaller and the metal gets stronger — which is why smiths have hammered steel for three thousand years.

Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. He demonstrated it to Napoleon, who made him a count and put him on the currency.

Ohm published his law in 1827 and German academics dismissed it as a web of naked fancies. He resigned his teaching post in disgust. Recognition came fifteen years later, from England, and eventually the unit.

Pascal built a working mechanical calculator at nineteen to help his father, a tax official, with endless sums. He also founded probability theory, largely by answering a gambler's question about how to split an interrupted bet.

A newton is roughly the weight of a medium apple in your hand — a coincidence physicists enjoy rather too much given the story about the tree. Newton himself told that story late in life, and only about seeing an apple fall.

James Joule was a brewer who did physics on the side, and he measured heat with the precision of someone used to controlling fermentation. On his honeymoon he reportedly took a thermometer to a waterfall to see if the falling water warmed up.

William Thomson realised there must be a coldest possible temperature and built a scale that starts there, so nothing is ever negative. He took his title from the river Kelvin, which ran past his Glasgow laboratory.

Michael Faraday left school at thirteen and worked as a bookbinder, reading the books he was binding. He became the finest experimentalist of the century and turned down both a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.
Joseph Henry discovered electromagnetic induction before Faraday did, but he was teaching a full timetable at a small American academy and published late. Faraday got the credit; Henry got the unit.

Hertz proved radio waves exist. Asked what use they might be, he said none whatsoever — it is just an experiment that proves Maxwell was right. Within fifteen years Marconi was sending signals across the Atlantic.

Becquerel expected sunlight to make uranium salts glow, so when the weather turned cloudy he shut everything in a drawer with a photographic plate. Days later the plate was fogged anyway. He had found radioactivity by being rained off.

Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes; anyone wanting to read them must sign a waiver.

Roentgen called them X-rays because he did not know what they were. The first radiograph was of his wife's hand; she looked at her own skeleton and said she had seen her death. He refused to patent any of it.

Told as a schoolboy to add the numbers from 1 to 100, Gauss saw that they pair up into fifty sums of 101 and answered almost immediately. He went on to contribute to nearly every branch of mathematics there was.

Wilhelm Weber built a working telegraph line across Gottingen with Gauss in 1833, years before commercial telegraphy. He was later dismissed from his professorship for refusing to swear an oath to the king.

Werner von Siemens built his first telegraph business on a loan from a cousin and turned it into one of the largest electrical firms in the world. The unit of conductance is the reciprocal of the ohm — and it used to be called the mho.

Rudolf Diesel designed an engine that ignites fuel by compression alone, with no spark. In 1913 he boarded a ferry across the English Channel and was never seen again; his body was found floating ten days later.

Elisha Otis did not invent the elevator — he invented the brake that catches it. At the 1854 World's Fair he had himself hoisted up, then ordered the rope cut. The platform dropped a few inches and stopped.

Richard Gatling wrote that he built it hoping one man could do the work of a hundred, so armies would need fewer soldiers and fewer would die. It is among the worst predictions anyone has ever made about a weapon.
Samuel Colt is said to have got the idea for the revolving cylinder watching a ship's wheel lock into position as it turned. He carved his first model out of wood on that voyage, aged sixteen.

The rifle made the family fortune. Sarah Winchester, the widowed heir, spent decades adding rooms to a California mansion — stairs to nowhere, doors opening onto walls — in a house that still stands and can still be visited.
Henry Deringer spelled his name with one r. Rival manufacturers copying his pocket pistol added a second to dodge the trademark, and the misspelling is the version that survived into the dictionary.

The Family Shakespeare removed everything Thomas Bowdler thought unsuitable to read aloud. His sister Henrietta did most of the editing but published anonymously, so the brother's name became the word for censoring a text.

Franz Mesmer claimed to heal patients by redirecting an invisible fluid he called animal magnetism. A royal commission including Benjamin Franklin investigated and found no fluid — but noticed the patients often got better anyway.

Jean Nicot was a French ambassador who sent tobacco seeds to the queen as a headache remedy. The plant, the genus and the addictive chemical inside it all ended up carrying the name of a diplomat who never smoked.

Linnaeus named the whole tobacco genus after Jean Nicot. It is a large family — tobacco's relatives include the tomato, the potato, the aubergine and deadly nightshade, all in the same botanical clan.

Named for Anders Dahl, a Swedish student of Linnaeus. The tubers were brought from Mexico to Europe partly as a possible food crop to replace the potato. Nobody liked the taste, so it was kept for the flowers.

Leonhart Fuchs died in 1566, nearly two centuries before the flower was found and named for him. The colour is named after the flower, so a sixteenth-century German doctor is the reason a shade of pink has that spelling.

Pierre Magnol invented the idea of the plant family — grouping species by shared structure rather than listing them alphabetically. Magnolias themselves are older than bees, and are pollinated by beetles instead.

Alexander Garden was a Scottish-born naturalist working in Charleston who sent specimens back to Europe for years. He was rewarded with a flower he had nothing to do with discovering — and which does not grow where he lived.

Georg Kamel was a Jesuit missionary and pharmacist in the Philippines. Linnaeus latinised his name to Camellus for the flower. Tea comes from the same genus, so every cup you drink is technically a camellia.

Michel Begon was a French colonial governor who collected plants and sponsored botanists. He never saw the flower named after him — it was named by a monk he had once employed, years after Begon's death.

Joel Poinsett was the first United States minister to Mexico and sent cuttings home in 1828. The Mexican name is flor de nochebuena, Christmas Eve flower — rather better than naming it after a visiting diplomat.

William Forsyth was royal head gardener at Kensington and a founder of what became the Royal Horticultural Society. He also sold the government a tree-wound plaster that turned out not to work, which caused a considerable scandal.

Johann Gottfried Zinn was an anatomist who mapped the structures of the human eye, and died at thirty-two having also written on Mexican plants. There is a zone of the eye named after him as well as the flower.

Named for Caspar Wistar — with an a. The botanist who named it spelled it with an e, nobody corrected him, and two centuries later we all still misspell an anatomist's surname every time we mention the flower.
This one is a trap. It looks like somebody called Philo Dendron, but it is plain Greek: philo-dendron, tree-loving, because the plant climbs. Not every scientific-sounding plant name hides a person.

Sylvester Graham was a minister who preached that bland food calmed the passions and that spices were dangerous. His cracker was designed to be dull on purpose. Modern versions are sweetened, which would have appalled him.

Graham insisted flour should keep the whole grain, bran and all, against the fashion for fine white flour. He was wrong about the moral effects and right about the nutrition, which is a better record than most food reformers manage.

Caesar Cardini ran a restaurant in Tijuana and was overwhelmed on the Fourth of July, 1924. Running short of ingredients, he threw what was left into a bowl and tossed it at the table for show. No Roman emperor was involved.
Nobody can prove the Duke of Wellington ever ate it. The name may simply be patriotic, or may come from the dish's resemblance to a brown boot. The duke has better claims to fame elsewhere.
In 1943 Ignacio Anaya was closing up when a group of American army wives arrived hungry. He fried some tortilla, added cheese and jalapeno, and served it. Ignacio's nickname was Nacho.

In 1889 a Naples pizzaiolo made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the one in the colours of the new Italian flag — red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil — and he named it after her.

Created for the ballerina Anna Pavlova during a tour, and claimed by both Australia and New Zealand ever since. A researcher combing old cookbooks found the earliest recipe in New Zealand, which has settled nothing.

Franz Sacher invented it at sixteen, standing in for a sick head chef. A later dispute between two Viennese firms over who could call theirs the original ran for seven years in court and is still called the Sweet Seven Years.

Named for the Stroganovs, one of the wealthiest families in imperial Russia. Their chef is credited with the dish, possibly designed so that beef could be cut thin and cooked fast in a Russian winter kitchen.

Bergamot-scented tea named for a British prime minister who almost certainly never blended anything. The likeliest explanation is that a merchant used his name to sell it, which worked so well it outlasted his politics.
American soldiers in Italy found espresso too strong and added hot water. Italian baristas named the result after them, not entirely as a compliment. It is now on the menu in Italy too.

Every origin story for the martini is contested: a town called Martinez in California, a vermouth brand called Martini and Rossi, a bartender of the same name. The drink is older than any reliable record of it.

The duke asked his shoemaker for a boot that was tough enough for the battlefield and neat enough for the evening. It became so fashionable that gentlemen wore them everywhere. The rubber version came decades later.

Lord Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo and had his coats cut with the sleeve running in one piece to the collar, so he could dress himself more easily. The design turned out to be better for movement and became standard sportswear.

Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built it to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and twice nearly died of arsenic poisoning — chemistry was a rougher trade then.

Avogadro's idea was ignored for nearly fifty years, and he died before it was accepted. The number itself — about six hundred thousand billion billion — was calculated by others and named in his honour afterwards.

Squeeze a gas into half the space and its pressure doubles. Boyle worked it out with a J-shaped glass tube and a quantity of mercury, and published it in 1662 while helping to invent the whole idea of the experiment.

Jacques Charles worked out that gases expand as they warm — and he was also a balloonist, making the first hydrogen balloon flight in 1783. Villagers where it landed attacked it with pitchforks, believing it was a monster.

John Dalton was colour blind and wrote the first scientific description of the condition, using himself as the subject. He asked for his eyes to be examined after his death; they are still preserved in Manchester.

A rare potassium mineral found near volcanic vents on Vesuvius, named for Avogadro. It is one of the quieter honours in science — a man who waited fifty years for recognition, given a mineral almost nobody has seen.

Friedrich Mohs ranked minerals one to ten by which scratches which — talc at one, diamond at ten. It measures nothing absolute, only the order. A fingernail is about 2.5, which is why it will mark gypsum but not glass.

Each whole step is about thirty-two times more energy, so a magnitude 7 is not slightly worse than a 6 — it is thirty-two times worse. Richter built the scale for southern California and it was adopted worldwide.

Mercalli measured what an earthquake does rather than how much energy it releases — from barely felt up to total destruction. Two places at the same Richter magnitude can be far apart on Mercalli, depending on what was built there.

An engineer and a meteorologist built it together: Saffir was studying how buildings fail in high wind, Simpson ran the National Hurricane Center. Categories 1 to 5 describe damage, not just wind speed.

Launched in 1990 with a mirror ground to the wrong shape by less than the width of a hair. Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993 — effectively giving a telescope spectacles — and it has been working ever since.

Copernicus is said to have received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not only astronomy; it was the moment humanity stopped being at the centre of anything.

James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817, in an essay of sixty-six pages based on six patients — some of whom he had only observed walking past in the street. His name was attached decades after his death.

Hans Asperger described the pattern in 1944. The term is being retired from clinical use in favour of the wider autism spectrum, both because the boundary proved hard to draw and because later research into his wartime conduct raised serious concerns.
